utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution is still continuing with their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. We are continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bicic. Let us return to September 4th, 1992, the day that you were exchanged. Now, you're sitting on a bus. In what city or location is that bus?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bus was in Bosanska Gradiska in front of the bridge, right by the bridge, by a park. That's where it was parked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, where was that bus in relation to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is across the river Sava.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you're right across -- Croatia is right across the river; you're right on the border at this point?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how long did you spend at the border waiting?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got there between 12.00 and 1.00, so sometime around midday. We waited there until about 5.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 5.00 in the afternoon, several other buses turned up. I don't know where they came from. And then all together we started off across the bridge, or rather, across the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Prior to being exchanged, did you see any of the defendants at that location?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was sitting across the street in a cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: At any point did he do anything in relation to the exchange?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, because I was sitting in the bus, so I didn't move from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How many people were on that bus?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many of us, and many of us sat on the floor. There weren't enough seats for the number of people that were there. I can't give you the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. At some point you leave the bus. Did you receive an order to leave the bus?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't leave the bus while we were waiting to be exchanged. We were shut up in the bus, actually. We were just sitting inside, waiting in front of the bridge, as I said, from 12.00 noon to about 5.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. At 5.00 in the afternoon, does the bus go over the bridge? Do you walk over the bridge? What happens?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The bus drove on, I would say, for another half hour, perhaps a little more, towards the motorway. And at a broken-down petrol station, we waited for some more time, and then we got out of the bus and the exchange started.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. At that point, at the petrol station, did you see any of the defendants here?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what was Miroslav Tadic doing?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had some papers in his hands and was talking to some people. Talking, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were standing outside in groups as each bus turned up, and then the exchange started, so that I crossed over to the other side, over a sort of invisible line, if I could put it that way. I stepped over the line where there were some other buses, and that's where we were gathered. They collected us up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when this exchange occurred, people were crossing each way, where was Mr. Tadic and what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't actually pay attention to where he was much, but I do know that he had some papers in his hands and was probably coordinating something. I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You cross into Croatia. What happens next, Mr. Bicic? Tell the Court. One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one correction in the translation. The third line -- third page, tenth, or rather, twelfth line, the witness said that he was negotiating, or rather, that he was talking to some people, whereas in English, it says "was talking." So could that be clarified? The witness said "negotiating" when he describes what Miroslav Tadic was doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. I'm sure the Prosecution will clear that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, at some point you indicate that the defendant Tadic had some papers in his hand and he was speaking or negotiating. Could you tell as best you could what exactly he was doing? Was he negotiating? Was he speaking? Was he giving orders? Please tell us all what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say with any certainty, because I was about ten metres away or maybe more from that particular spot. I saw several people there who were talking to him. Now, what they were talking about, I really can't say. I can't clarify that, because I didn't hear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you cross into Croatia. What happens? Tell the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They put us onto the buses and drove us off towards Slavonski -- or rather, Bosanski Brod. They dropped me off at Slavonski Brod, at the hospital there, where they examined me and gave me medical assistance. They kept me -- they wanted to keep me there for treatment, but my brother and my friends came to fetch me, so that I left the hospital and went to stay with friends, to their homes, and stayed there for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: At any point during the exchange, did you meet anyone? Was anyone waiting for you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My brother's friends were waiting for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They put me in front of some television cameras - Croatian television I'm referring to - and I gave a brief statement about what had happened in the camps that I was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you see any relatives there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In one of the buses - I learned later on that it came from Doboj - but anyway, in that bus I saw my mother's sister and her husband and their son. When I went up to them, they couldn't recognise me. They were shocked and they kept looking at me, and it was only when we started talking that they recognised my voice and realised that it was me. So we had a chat. And they were expelled from Doboj themselves and had been exchanged at the same spot in Dragalic, like me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: These relatives that didn't recognise you, had you seen them very often prior to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My aunt, my mother's sister, had spent some 15 years living with us together in Samac. That's where she worked in the social accounting service, the SDK. And after that, we would visit each other at least twice a month. They would come to see us or we would go to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say they couldn't recognise you, had you lost weight? Had your face changed? Were you beaten at the time? Why couldn't they recognise you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I had lost quite a bit of weight, and also because my face was all swollen from all -- and it was all black and blue, and my nose was broken. So I suppose that's why they could hardly recognise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How much weight had you lost?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was -- before I was detained, I weighed between 116 [Realtime transcript read in error "160"] and 120 kilos. When I was exchanged, and in the hospital, when I weighed myself there, I weighed 63 kilos.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the transcript says "between 160 and 120." Is that 116, or is that ...

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One hundred and sixteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you indicated that you were on Croatian television at the time of exchange.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: At this point, Your Honour, could we play approximately ten seconds of the clip which is Prosecution's Exhibit number 27, just to have him identify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: P27. It's already in the audiovisual room. Turn to the video evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you have any question about that? That's definitely you, Mr. Bicic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, I'd like to briefly discuss your financial loss. You indicated that you owned an arcade or games shop in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you describe what type of property you had in that shop and what happened to it.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the shop I had about 20 machines, gaming machines and entertainment machines, and the machines included billiards, flippers, video games, and poker machines.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what happened to it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It disappeared, all of it. I don't know. Apart from that, we had about 150 machines all in all, which we rented out to other establishments for entertainment: billiards, football, table football, video games, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what happened to those 150 video games?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Quite simply, they're no longer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated, sir, that near your home you had a building that was under construction.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Adjoining my house I had built another catering establishment which was nearing completion. Construction work was almost finished. And so some tiles remained in the pallets that they came in, which I was going to put down on the floors, and I had some brass shelving that I was going to put up inside, and quite a lot of other construction material that I was going to build into the interior of the establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What happened to it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is it still there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That catering enterprise and part of my house was destroyed. There is nothing in the house: no doors, no windows, no water pipes or cables, electricity cables, or anything like that, or parquet floors, let alone the furniture and all the other things that were in it. That has all disappeared. And the house was devastated, completely destroyed. Almost half the house was knocked down; how, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your wife had a boutique. Tell us about that, please.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my wife did have a boutique. It was a container-type kiosk boutique in the centre of town, opposite the hotel. There were some 20 kiosks of the same shape and size, and there were different shops in the kiosks. There were boutiques, several boutiques with clothing, then there were hairdressing salons, florist shops, bakeries, and so on. This was that section of the centre of town, and it was called the Mini Trade Centre, this row of kiosks. And in one of the boutiques they also sold leather goods: handbags, belts, and the like, made of leather.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What happened to these boutiques?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I couldn't tell you. But last year a friend of mine whom I sent a power of attorney that the boutique, which is still located in Samac, that he should transfer it to where he was, to the Domaljevac-Samac municipality -- however, despite all the attempts to do so, he was not permitted to; he was not allowed to do that. And then somebody transferred the boutique to a nearby village, Tisina. When my friend attempted to repossess it, he was expelled from the yard in which the boutique was located and they asked him to pay some money for them to give it back to him, allegedly. However, sometime in the early spring of this year the boutique -- the people who had appropriated the boutique set it up at a crossroads towards Orasje and Domaljevac, and at the junction towards Obudovac, at a turning there, then my friend and some other people, with a big dredger, lifted the boutique or kiosk, loaded it up onto a truck with this crane, and transported it to his own back yard, the back yard of the house he still lives in today. After that, they called him over the phone and asked allegedly to be remunerated for the boutique. They said that they had done some repairs to it. However, I heard from others, learnt from others, that the boutique had in fact been used for several years by a policeman, or rather, a police technician, from Samac, who still works in the police force in Samac, and he himself asked my friend to pay him some money for the renovations that he had allegedly done. He wanted four or five hundred marks for this. But my friend had all the paperwork that I had certified, or rather, my wife had authenticated the papers, so that when the police came to establish what had occurred in respect of this kiosk, he supplied all the necessary papers. The police was able to see that everything was in order, that they were all regularly kept and he no longer had any problems with it. But the kiosk itself is ruined -- ruined quite a lot. Everything that was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. inside it has disappeared, including the shelves and mirrors, of course the goods that were in it too. It was dented and broken. So one would have to invest quite a bit of additional money to get it working again, put it in shape, in proper repair.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, all of the property that you, your wife, and your brother lost, did you ever receive any sort of receipt or certificate for this property and/or did you ever receive any compensation for people either taking it or using it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We never received any receipt that it had been taken away from us, nor were we ever asked about any compensation. Quite simply, they just asked us to buy it again, to buy back our property, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, last question on property: Approximately how much money were you and your family worth prior to April 17th?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to assess the value, but we had four establishments, catering establishments. We were the owners of three, and one of them I had refurbished completely. I had invested a great deal of money into that one. As I already said, we also had about 150 different machines, gaming machines and others. Then we had the pizzeria, which was one of the best restaurants in those parts, and well known beyond the region as well. The value of all that property was enormous for those circumstances, for the circumstances we lived in and for those standards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you have when you got out, when you were -- when you and your brother were exchanged? What did you have?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had I don't know whose T-shirt on me and trousers which somebody had brought me so that I could be exchanged in a decent change of clothing and not in bloodstained, dirty clothes, the kind that I was in. That was all that I had. And my brother left looking like I had just described, dirty, like I was, in a blood -- in bloodstained clothing which he was wearing, the only clothes that he had on his back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The question I had was: You had an enormous amount of property and financial holdings. At the time of your release, what did you have financially?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know because I did not have occasion to see, but when my brother went to check over all the things and when he asked that our property be returned, he told me -- and, in fact, took photographs of this house of ours, which had been half not -- destroyed, and the shop, the pizzeria that they asked him money for, to buy back the things that were inside, his own things, and he told them that they were welcome to it all and that we would buy other things. He saw the boutique somewhere near the banks of the Sava River, behind the hotel. It had been left there, abandoned. But when we were supposed to get it back, it was transported to Tisina, which is a neighbouring village to Samac, and they also asked to be paid some money for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. I wonder whether, Mr. Bicic, you could clarify about bank accounts. Did you have bank accounts with money left in those accounts when you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We had bank accounts, business accounts, with money on them, but the documents and booklets we didn't have on us. Some of these were left behind in our house. And in the barracks in Brcko, they seized absolutely everything we had on us, all the documents, starting from our ID's, driving licences, and everything else we had in our pockets. So that, I don't know. I simply don't know what happened with those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Just one further question: Did you attempt to follow up after you were released until today, follow up with those banking institutions concerning what had been in those accounts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I haven't been to Bosanski Samac at all since I was exchanged. My brother did go back, but I don't know whether he made any such attempts. We never discussed it. And I believe that the Jugobanka which used to exist in those days, as well as the Sarajevska Banka in Samac, they probably have no data there, and one doesn't really know whom one could address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And whatever papers you had, identity papers, papers that you could have used at the bank, were taken from Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Brcko, all of us were deprived of everything we had on us. This didn't apply just to me and my brother but absolutely everyone who was transferred there. And when they took us inside, one by one, into the premises of the barracks, or rather, the prison in that barracks, then they leant us against the walls, searched our pockets. They even took off our shoes. Some people even had to strip as far as their underwear to make sure that they were not concealing anything. And whatever they found was thrown into a pile. What happened to that later, I don't know. Anyway, we were never given any of it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to go from there, your financial loss, to your physical condition on being released. You indicated you were checked at a hospital, and you also mentioned previously that you had received medical care. Let's start off with your head and your face. Could you please describe the injuries that you had, beginning with your head and your face?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My head, I have several scars. One is right up here at the top; it is about 5 or 6 centimetres long. The other one is to the left side of my head, the injury above my left eye. A broken nose, teeth, the right side of my face, my right eye, with which I am having problems. After this exchange, for two years the right side of my face and my right eye were affected, so that the treatment took almost two years. I had a twitch on that part of my face. And even now when the weather changes, that part of my face goes numb and I often lose control over the mucus in my mouth. Then here on the chin too I have a big scar. My saliva starts coming out uncontrolled. I also had problems with my urinary tract, but that was also treated by doctors. But maybe the worst of all is the still existing traumas, the nightmares, so that I sleep very briefly at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's just take a step back for a moment. What about your hearing and your eyesight? Could you comment upon that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My eyesight has deteriorated quite a bit in relation to what it was before, that is, the period prior to my detention. But now, on my right eye, I see much worse. The left eye is also damaged but not to that extent. My vision has been reduced. As regards my hearing, on one occasion when they beat me, from my left ear blood started running, and the hearing in my left ear is impaired in relation to my right ear. Doctors treated me for this as far as they were able, but still to this day I have a hearing problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, let's take the body: the neck, the shoulders, the chest, the ribs. What, if any, injuries did you suffer in the area of the body, the trunk portion of the body?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have eight broken ribs. When the weather changes, I have bad pains in the rib area and in my back, frequently my neck goes stiff; and I must repeat that's mostly when there's a change of weather. My right kidney has been damaged. It has been moved from the blows.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, let's talk about your legs, your feet, and your hands, any injuries.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On my right hand, my little finger was broken. On my feet, I don't have any serious injuries, but from the blows they received [as interpreted], they hurt me frequently. I feel pain in my legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that you've suffered injuries all over your body, from head to toe basically. Did you have any of these injuries or problems prior to your incarceration in this case?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's finally talk about psychologically. You indicated that you sleep less. Tell us what it was like that period right after you were exchanged and the time following that, up to today. Tell us what it's been like, sir, for you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first it was very hard. For almost two years I had very bad pains, almost whenever I moved; and then gradually, after taking medication, the pain gradually subsided and became less pronounced. And as I was saying, only when the weather changes abruptly, then the pain reappears. My nerves, of course, are also not what they used to be after all this, so that, as I say, I sleep little. I get these nightmares, so that I take some pills. I also smoke more heavily than I used to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did any of these problems you've just described exist prior to your being arrested and detained in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examination. Is anybody going to cross-examine the witness? Yes, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will start with cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On behalf of Mr. Zaric's Defence, therefore -- one second. Your Honours, before I start with cross-examining this witness, I believe this is the right moment to tender one document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Which document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Actually, it is the official translation of the statement of Mr. Hasan Bicic, who was our previous witness. We just entered an unofficial version, so we have received an official version and I would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Which statement is this one, if I may -- you made it where? What is the number it has already been exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The number is D84.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. Can we just check with the Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. The B/C/S version was submitted as D8/4, and there was a provisional English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have that one formally numbered, please? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon Mr. Bicic. My name is Aleksandar Lazarevic. I represent Mr. Simo Zaric. I will be cross-examining you. But before I start with my questions, I should like, on behalf of my client, to express regret for everything that you went through during the war and all the bad things that happened to you. If I may now, I would just like to ask you to go back to the situation as it was in Bosanski Samac a couple of months prior to the outbreak of the conflict, that is, prior to the 17th of April, 1992. Would it be right to say that prior to the outbreak of the conflict, the atmosphere in town was tense, as a result of numerous acts of sabotage and incidents that had occurred in the territory of Samac? Can that be said, or not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer would be that there were some incidents, such as the destruction of some long-distance cables across the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, we will come back to that topic. My question relates simply to the atmosphere among the people of Bosanski Samac at the time. Was there some tension or fear felt by the people at the time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say no rather than yes, because in the establishments that we had, I had contact with all our guests, belonging to all ethnic groups from our town. Some were tense, others were not, during those couple of months. But there were people who were not tense, who did not believe that a conflict would occur in the town itself, that is, in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, but I'm just asking you about the feelings of the majority of citizens. I'm not asking you about individuals. I'm, rather, referring to the general climate in town.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, probably. Probably there was tension. That would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now go on to certain incidents that occurred at the time. I will just ask you to confirm whether they occurred or not and whether this had an impact on the atmosphere among the people of Bosanski Samac. Can we agree in saying that, among other incidents, there was the one in which two young men were killed, two young men of Muslim ethnicity, and a young woman of Serb ethnicity in the Valentino Cafe? Did this incident occur?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was an incident, but I can't really remember. Yes, near the Sava, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did this cause a disturbance among the people, the fact that two young men had been killed and a young woman wounded?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a lot of talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let me ask you about another incident in which a police patrol of the reserve police were wounded, three persons. I'll give you their names: Nizam Ramusovic, Mirsad Mesic, and Danilo Vitomir. Did that incident also occur?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that some policemen - I don't know which - had engaged in an exchange of fire with someone, probably these people you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this incident also provoke a reaction among the people, a feeling of insecurity among the people, when people were shot and wounded?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And let me ask you about just one more incident. There were many more, but I don't wish to take up too much time. Can we agree that sometime in the end of March in 1992 barricades were set up in Samac? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was a Wednesday, which was the market day in Samac, and I was working in our pizzeria when I heard that some barricades had been put up, that people were not allowed to enter town by car but only on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That's what I had in mind. Would you agree that those barricades were put up by members of the Party of Democratic Action?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not able to tell you that because I was not interested in those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel, you have to wait for the witness to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. complete his sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, can it be said that at the time, there was large-scale, illegal arming of citizens in the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which citizens you have in mind when you say large-scale arming by the citizens, because some citizens received weapons from the Yugoslav People's Army, and I'm mostly referring to citizens of Serb ethnicity and members of the 4th Detachment, whereas the majority of people, like my brother, had to or were forced to buy weapons for themselves with which they would perhaps protect their property and themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, I primarily had in mind the people who were, through the army -- who were not issued weapons by the army or the police. I had in mind physical persons who were not members of the army or the police. Those are the people I had in mind. But I think you've already given me an answer. So it follows from your answer, I think, that your brother, Hasan Bicic, purchased two automatic rifles of the Kalashnikov brand, with three sets of ammunition. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he bought them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: When I said "procured," I meant "bought." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've given you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bicic, I should like to move on to another area now, and that is Territorial Defence. You said before this Trial Chamber that with Alija Fitozovic, you discussed the topic of territorial defence and that he asked you whether you wished to join the Territorial Defence, which would be composed of the members of all ethnic groups living in the region, as well as the 4th Detachment, which belonged to the JNA. Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember, and I did say that if all three nations and members of that 4th Detachment were in that Territorial Defence, then he could subscribe me to that too, write my name down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I completely agree that you put it that way, that that is what you said. I should now like to remind you of something else that you said, and that is that this conversation took place in front of his office, not far from your pizza parlour, perhaps some 50 metres away. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we then agree that that conversation that you had with Mr. Alija Fitozovic took place in front of the building in which the Islamic religious community was housed? Is that the same building?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the building --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't finished answering.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a building which lies in the street leading towards my pizzeria, or rather, our pizzeria, some 50 metres away? I do not know whether it was the building -- that is, there were boutiques there, there were some apartments and offices. Now, those offices, who they belonged to, I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you one more thing: Was it the building where the SDA party headquarters were located?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There was a bakery. So it was a small building with small offices, and a boutique, a bakery, and I can't remember all the other things that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because I have a piece of information according to which Mr. Alija Fitozovic, before the war, worked in the electrical company, electricity company, and that, if you agree with me, is about a kilometre away from your pizzeria. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before, he worked in the electricity company, but then - electricity board - but then he told me that he had moved to the Territorial Defence and that he was head of Territorial Defence. That was his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we now have a very full picture of all this. In connection with your conversation with Alija Fitozovic, did you discuss the conversation with your kum, Stipo Cerlinski?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Stipo Cerlinski tell you that he had some reservations with respect to that and that the 4th -- especially with respect to the fact that the 4th Detachment would become a part of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stipo Cerlinski, my kum, told me that he doubted very much that the 4th Detachment would also come under the composition of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that's what I meant when I said "had reservations."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, I wonder whether you might get the witness to tell us what a "kum" is, a k-u-m, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, for the Trial Chamber, I should like to ask you to explain the term and concept of "kum."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our parts, "kum" means a witness at a wedding ceremony, so he was a witness, with his wife, at the wedding ceremony of me and my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bicic. I think that is sufficient explanation. Let us now move on to another topic, the Territorial Defence and the moment that you were already being held in the Territorial Defence building. In your statement, you described the circumstances under which Dikan was killed and also how Lugar took you and your brother out, you and your brother Hasan, how he took you to the yard of the TO and threatened you with death. Do you agree that there was a realistic danger of you being killed had you stayed on in the TO building? Was that a realistic danger?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as in any other camp, the camp that we passed through, the danger was always present, that at every moment, every second, when people turned up to beat us and ill-treat us, we felt the danger looming over us, the danger that they might kill us with all the beatings and blows or, quite simply, with their weapons or implements that they used.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bicic. My question referred to the TO building, when you were in the TO building and when you were present at the events that took place there. Was there a clear and realistic danger that you would be killed, you and your brother, the two of you who were in the yard?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did exist, quite certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We are -- let's stay with the TO building in Samac. We are still there. And I want to ask you this: Did that danger exist -- was there that threat for the other people in the TO? Did the danger exist for them too? Could they have been killed too, just like that unfortunate Dikan?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they could have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I should like now to move on and dwell for a moment on your stay in the military barracks at Brcko. According to your statement, nobody beat you there, you personally. I'm asking about you personally. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except the first night when I arrived and when I received several blows to my back and when they tied my hands behind my back. But after that, nobody beat me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You describe this in your statement as being pushed more.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but also with kicks, with knees in my back, and I was tied. It wasn't actually pushing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't say that they were very gentle. I'm not claiming that. Let me just ask you: You say you were able to wash; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, several days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You did not have to sing Chetnik songs there, did you, or as my learned friend of the Prosecution termed them, Serbian patriotic songs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You told us about the event when you sang the Yugoslav hymn and you said that you sang it in one breath and that you were surprised.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were shocked, so we sang it from start to finish in a single breath.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you felt relieved compared to what the situation was like in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at one given moment, as far as the song was concerned, we did, and the fact that we weren't beaten any more. However, there, too, there was a brandishing of weapons, a machine-gun actually, a heavy machine-gun that had been posed on some tracks in the corridor some 20 metres away -- which was some 20 metres long. So we weren't particularly safe there either, because the people would aim that heavy machine-gun at us, the people in uniform, in the JNA army uniform, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: May we take it, then, that some of the prisoners who were transferred from the TO building to Brcko were given a certain amount of medical assistance there? In Brcko, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nalic received assistance and several other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we agree that the conditions of your stay at the barracks in Brcko were significantly better than what they had been in the TO building in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the first few days, but the last two or three days that we spent there, the conditions were actually the same, and there were 50 of us in a small room, so we were not all able to sit down. Some of us had to stand while others sat. But that was to begin with. But several days after we had bathed and been interrogated and given some statements, those of us who had given statements were then transferred to another cell, a similar cell, but we were given a blanket there to cover ourselves with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that we can say that in that second period, in the second half of your stay, the conditions were a bit better, significantly better?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not significantly better, but a bit better, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to ask you about the conduct towards you in Brcko, how people behaved towards you, that is to say, on the part of the people who were in charge of you. Did these people behave better towards you than the people who held you at the TO building in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, better, somewhat better.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And finally, to round off this topic, let me ask you the following: May we agree that your transfer from the Territorial Defence building in Samac to the barracks in Brcko did away with the danger of you being killed? Did it do away with that threat, killed or terrorised by the Serbian special forces in Samac? Would that be correct to say?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That transfer did temporarily waylay the -- discard -- do away with the danger of the threat of Serbian special forces, but quickly after that, they took us towards Bijeljina, where we experienced the same things as we had done in the Territorial Defence building, almost identical events as far as the beatings were concerned and forcing us to sing and kneel and all the other kinds of mistreatment, and significant injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, I was just speaking about the transfer to Brcko, and I think you have already answered my question and said that that danger had been temporarily postponed.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would like to tender one document to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, can you describe it, if it has a date, and tell us whether the Prosecution have been given a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a statement of Mr. Bicic given to Mr. Zaric in the barracks in Brcko on 28 of April, 1992. This document was provided to the Defence by the Prosecutor, and we have here a B/C/S version and the provisional translation in English. We already gave this document to be officially translated, but we still haven't received it. So for the moment, I would like to have the number for B/C/S version and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Before we decide on the documents, we have already had a slight problem with provisional translations before, and if it's your intention to put the contents of the statement to the witness, it's important that we have a full -- the acceptable translation in English, because sometimes counsel or ourselves, as the Trial Chamber, get misled.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I fully understand your words, Your Honour, and I believe that this translation is pretty correct. As I have already said, we gave this document to be translated by the official service here in the Tribunal, and actually we expected to receive it today, but unfortunately it wasn't finished yet. Also, I would like maybe to hear the opinion of the OTP, because we gave them this translation, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'll hear from the OTP. But on the translation, we should not waste time, because we can use the Serbo-Croat if there are passages read out loud by yourself or the witness and then our interpreters can deal with the problem and then we can receive the official translation, the English one, much later, rather than have the provisional one. I would like to hear from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it would help the Chamber, we, during discovery, provided a final translation, an English copy. We have both the B/C/S version and a final version or a certified translation. I have two here. That's all I have. I didn't expect to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So you have the formal English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think we should get that copy for the Registry, and that's the copy the Trial Chamber will use. So we will have the Serbo-Croat and the formal English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No objection. But once again, we weren't prepared to file several copies of the English translation today, but I could provide them tomorrow for the Court. I'd be happy to -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. So counsel can proceed with the statement. Can we have the copies so that we have the formal numbering and all the parties concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one for counsel, and we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The English?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, a copy for counsel in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So we'll get the Serbo-Croat from the Defence counsel and then the formal English from the -- the formal English translation from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is a real way of cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, these are statements which are not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We can go ahead. Let's have the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be numbered Defence Exhibit D9/4 ter and the English D9/4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bicic, I should like to ask you to take a look at the document before you. It is a two-page document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it has two pages. But it is fairly illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for that. Perhaps I'll be able to help you. On the first page, in the right-hand corner, do you see the signature "Muhamed Bicic"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Would you now take a look at page 2, the lower left-hand corner. Does it say "Muhamed Bicic" there too?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On page 2. Page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Would you take a look at the document now, please.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can take a look, but I'm sure that you yourself can see that it is not very legible. I haven't got my glasses with me, so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I didn't think that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe that copy can be given to the witness for purposes of Defence counsel's questions, so that the witness can easily read, if possible, although he has said that he hasn't got his glasses. Maybe what you can do, if there are passages, like I said before, you point out where the passages are to the witness and then you do the reading, all right, slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Your Honour. I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bicic, is this the statement which you gave at the barracks in Brcko to Simo Zaric on the 28th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the suggestion just made by the Trial Chamber and Her Honour, I should like to quote some details from the statement, and you will say whether that is what it says, yes or no, for the record. Then I will ask you something with respect to those details. In paragraph 1 of that statement, and the line is line 9 -- I'm going to read it out to you and you try to follow, just to tell me whether I've read it out properly: "My brother Hasan, in early April, via some connections -- through some of his connections, purchased two Kalashnikov automatic rifles with three ammunition magazines each, and paid 700 German marks for them each." Have I read this out correctly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume you have, but I haven't got my glasses, as I say, and I can't see the words clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, what I have just stated, did you say the same thing before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you have just quoted, yes, I did say that my brother Hasan bought two -- purchased two automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That was my question. Thank you. Now, the next sentence goes as follows: "In addition, I had a hunting rifle and a pistol, for which I had obtained permits from the SUP." Did you state that, too, here before the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did possess a hunting rifle and a pistol, and I had the necessary licences and papers that were issued in SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm not questioning that, Mr. Bicic. I'm just asking you whether you recounted that to the Trial Chamber, whether you said you had a hunting rifle and a pistol, with a licence to carry it. Have you ever told us that here in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've just said that I did have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I should like now to refer to a portion of your statement which says something in connection with Alija Fitozovic: "He called me to the TO office, to his office at the TO, and told us that a Territorial Defence was being set up in the town of Samac and that it would include all three nationalities, including the 4th Detachment of the JNA." Did you say that here as well?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in front of the office in which he worked - I don't know what kind of office it was - I said that we had talked about that and that I said to him that if all three nations, plus the 4th Detachment, became part of the Territorial Defence, then I would be happy to join that same organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I fully accept that. So that is, in principle, what you said here in the courtroom, that Alija Fitozovic said that members of all the nationalities would become members and that the 4th Detachment would too?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in front of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me read out now: "After that I spoke to Stipo Cerlinski, my kum, my best man, and he said he had some reservations about that unit, particularly that he doubted that the 4th JNA detachment formed in Bosanski Samac would join." So you have already told us that.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that he didn't believe that all these would join the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't wish to dwell extensively on this statement, but maybe just one further point. When speaking about the weapons seized from you when the special forces broke in, and you said, "We collected the weapons that we owned in one place in our house," that is also something that you have said here in Court.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, in our living room, on the floor of the living room.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: "And then we got into a Golf vehicle and went to the public security station, where we were detained."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't get in; we were forced in. They beat us and had their weapons pointed at our heads. And then they drove us in this Golf to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that's what you said, but in fact, you were arrested. They took you into custody and drove you to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And after that, you were incarcerated in the SUP building, or rather, the TO of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So that's what you told us here in Court: First you were detained in the SUP and then in the TO?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bicic, as far as your statement is concerned. I just wish to clarify a few points. I have just one more question for you. You have already said that when you gave this statement in Brcko, that no one beat you, that no one threatened you, and that this was, in fact, a frank conversation. So let me just ask you, in that connection: Would it be right to say that what you stated during that conversation is reflected in this statement? Or let me put it this way: Was the statement correctly drawn up, and does it reflect what you said there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't read the statement in its entirety, how correct it is, but my signature is there. We really did have a discussion. I was not beaten. We discussed also where we would go. I asked whether we could be released in Brcko, because there was no war ongoing there, but I was not given an answer. If that is what it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you have told us all that in the courtroom here, and it has all been recorded in the transcript. I wish to thank you for testifying. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before you sit down, Counsel, I just want to make it clear on the status of this statement and what the witness has said, because he hasn't read it. He had never read it, so other than the statements which you actually put to him, he can't be held against everything in the statement. Yes, that is clear. Okay. Any other counsel wishing to cross-examine the witness? I see none. Any re-examination? Oh, I'm sorry. Maybe I didn't wait for the translation. Yes. Any other counsel wishing to cross-examine the witness? Yes, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. May I just inquire are we working until 5.00, so I can adjust my cross-examination accordingly, or later? Because we were told that we would be working until 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I think all of us forgot that we were supposed to have a break. Let me find out from the interpreters and maybe from the Registry assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let me ask the interpreters whether it would be okay if we went on to 5.00, because there is 25 minutes more.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I think so, yes, Your Honour. We will manage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. So you can proceed. It just shows how relaxed all of us are this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And good afternoon, Mr. Bicic. My name is Dragan Krgovic. I'm one of the Defence counsel for Mr. Miroslav Tadic, and I have a few questions for you. I will not examine you in detail about the things that you have told us about in detail, your arrest and the treatment you received, but we will touch upon some other issues. So as we have some 20 minutes available, and we'd like to get through the cross-examination as quickly as possible, please give me a yes or no answer or just say that you don't know, if you don't know, and then we'll get through this more easily. First of all, Mr. Bicic, during your testimony here in court, you said that prior to the outbreak of the conflict, you and your brother had taken your families out of Samac?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did the other people, regardless of their ethnicity, take their families or parts of their families away to safety immediately prior to the outbreak of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but let me clear this up. On the 11th of April, there was a rally in Bosanski Samac, in the square in front of the boutique, that was owned by my wife and me. I was there close by, when the people going onto the stage or the podium speaking through the microphones could be heard, and they were accusing one another. Some people were pointing to their own families that were in front of them and asking others where their families were. And then my daughter told me, "School has been dismissed and we have been given marks as if we have completed our grades," even though school was supposed to continue for another two months before the holiday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that even before this rally that you just mentioned, people had taken away their families already?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Samac was mostly left without the Serbs, both in school as well as in town. Especially the women and children had left, whereas the adults stayed behind in town and could be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about members of the Croatian ethnic group? Did they take away their families too?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Tihic's family had left town just before that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let me move on to another topic, and that is the time you spent in the SUP building and the warehouse of the Territorial Defence. During your testimony, you said that from the SUP building, you were transferred to the TO building together with your brother, Sulejman Tihic, [redacted], and an old Albanian. Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and a few other men from the other premises of the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In the TO building, you spent some ten days or so, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: While you were in the TO warehouse, did you ever see Miroslav Tadic there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me now go on to the procedure of your exchange and the exchange itself. You said in your statement that at the playing field in front of the school, there were many citizens who came to see you off when you were being exchanged. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Unofficially, informally, people approached the playground and came up to about 10 metres from the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were citizens of all ethnic groups present who came to greet you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unable to answer that. There was simply a large group of men that were -- of people that were waving as we were leaving. We were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. called out, and as we were called out, we got into the buses. I was sitting on the side towards the school, so that I could only see over the heads of other people, as I was sitting on the floor, that is, between the rows of seats. So I could hardly see much, simply arms waving. So I don't know who it was who came to see us off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Who called out your names when you came out of the building that you were staying in?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who called us out was Sveto -- I forget his surname. He was a teacher, a Montenegrin, who lived in our town for many years and he was a teacher in the neighbouring village. I think he was a teacher in the village of Tisina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that it was Sveto Vasovic, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Vasovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Veljo Mastic perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Escorting those two buses that were taking you for the exchange, were there any police cars?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you. As I was saying, I was sitting on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you saw Mr. Tadic in Gradiska when you were at the parking lot there. Did you see Mr. Tadic in front of the school when you were entering the buses?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you were taken for the exchange, was Dragan Lukac with you in the bus?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was in another bus, in the other bus, if I'm not mistaken. I can't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Earlier, during your testimony, you described the time you spent in Bosanska Gradiska. Are you certain that no one got off the bus in Gradiska?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the bus that I sat in and got up in to stretch my legs, like all the other people, I didn't see anyone getting out, except Sveto and the driver. I don't know whether there was anyone else in the back, any other member of the escort who was accompanying us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: From your bus or from the other bus, did people go down, step down on the pavement, and some go to the toilet?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The people that were being taken to be exchanged did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see Dragan Lukac sitting in the cafe next to Miroslav Tadic and drinking beer?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But you did see Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Mr. Tadic with Mirko Pavic, my neighbour, and policeman, who used to be a policeman before, too, in the Samac police station, and with some other men who were also wearing either police uniforms or civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Simo Krunic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: He was also a policeman?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On page 3028 of your statement, you stated that in the gym of the elementary school, a large number of old people were brought in and that you knew many of them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The evening prior to the exchange?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You said that some of them were over 80 years old, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were some old grannies who could hardly walk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any one of those people who were over 80 years old?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not. They're mostly from the environs of Samac, so I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, when you reached the place for the exchange, were there any policemen that you may have seen in the cafe, or other policemen in uniform?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. During the actual exchange at the petrol station.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw men in uniform from UNPROFOR or whatever they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps see representatives of the International Community?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I just said, men from UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about the OSCE or something?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't really tell you exactly who they were, but anyway, they were foreign citizens, foreign nationals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were some of them representing the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, but I can't tell you. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mladen Borbeli?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean Mladjo --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about Stipo Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Alija Cosic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Alojz Balogh?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Lonac, Ivan?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He used to be a policeman or a police chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did they go to be exchanged together with you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some were with me in the bus, like Stipo, I think Borbeli. I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that they crossed into Croatia with you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, because when I was brought to the buses that were supposed to take us on, I was separated by my friends, put in a car, and driven off in the direction of Slavonski Brod. And at a petrol station some, perhaps, 10 kilometres away, my brother was waiting for me, and then they took me to have a bath first and tidy myself up, and then to the hospital. The others were transferred, I think, to Bosanski Brod. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in Dragalic, when you were being exchanged, Miroslav Tadic, or anyone else, asked you, asked people individually, whether they wanted to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, because I quickly separated from the group and joined these friends of mine. So I didn't rejoin the group again except when, close to the buses, I spotted my aunt and her husband and son.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where these people that I just mentioned are now? I'm referring to Mladen Borbeli, Stipo Vukovic, Alija Cosic, Alojz Balogh, and Ivan Lonac.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps whether they're living in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were met there by friends. Who did they learn from when you were coming? Do you know that, and did they tell you how they learnt about it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They attended each exchange, together with my brother, who kept waiting in the hope that I would appear in the group that was being exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you who they heard from when the exchange would take place?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there was a commission for the exchange of prisoners of the HDZ -- I'm sorry, of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I learnt that in hospital while I was being examined. I met some people who came to see me and greet me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of Mijo Matanovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard of him. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he was president of the Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War and Arrested Civilians of the Croatian Defence Council, the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that he worked in that team of people who were in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. I've finished my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we -- the Prosecution, will you be re-examining? Or is there somebody -- oh, Mr. Zecevic. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Me too. Me too, Madam President. Don't forget us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. We'll adjourn. I think we have overworked our interpreters. We will adjourn and continue our proceedings tomorrow at 0930 hours. And tomorrow, up to Friday, we shall follow the usual programme: 0930, and then, in the afternoon, 1530 hours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 31st day of October 2001, at 0930 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
